articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on the sidelines of APEC, White House says
articles.summary:
STORY: Leaders from across Asia-Pacific will gather in the Chinese city of Shenzhen next week for the APEC summit.

And all eyes are on a possible trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

So what is APEC, and what does it do?

:: What is APEC?

APEC, or the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, has 21 members.

Together, they make up about 62 percent of the global economy and around half of world trade.

It operates on non-binding commitments reached by consensus, with commitments made on a voluntary basis.

APEC calls its members "economies," not nations.

That lets Chinese-ruled Hong Kong and democratically governed Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its own territory, take part.

:: Why Shenzhen?

It's the third time China has hosted the summit, after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.

Shenzhen is China's tech hub, home to giants like BYD, Huawei and Tencent.

Analysts say the choice lets Beijing show off its vision for development and trade, and the city's resilience amid global turmoil.

:: Who is attending?

China hasn't officially said who's coming.

But Trump, Putin and the leaders of Canada, Australia, Mexico and Indonesia are also due to attend, among others.

:: What are the key issues?

The possible meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin could produce some sticking points.

According to analysts, China is reluctant to discuss nuclear disarmament because it has fewer such weapons than the other two.

The US and Russia will also be keen to discuss the Ukraine war, but not necessarily China, they said.

Then there's US-China relations.

A trade truce has been extended, but analysts say both sides are falling short on their promises.

Rare earths, artificial intelligence, tariffs and US arms sales to Taiwan are likely on the agenda.

The Middle East conflict is also expected to feature, with its toll on energy supplies, trade and prices.

And China's strained ties with Japan and the Philippines over Taiwan and the South China Sea.

The leaders' meeting runs November 18th and 19th, preceded by an annual summit of CEOs on the 17th and 18th.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers.

While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.

Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.

Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers.

Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran .

The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.

Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China .

The trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the "beginning of hopefully a conversation" on nuclear disarmament "that can be productive going forward," said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced.

But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.

Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to "step up ... to the adult table" on a matter of international importance.

Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit

By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige.

For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.

"I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.

More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia's war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.

The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.

"You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism," he said.

The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years

Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as "dear friend."

Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi .

Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.

As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia's energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.

In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a "no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv's Western allies played a part in provoking Russia's military action in Ukraine.

Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing's policy on issues related to Taiwan.

Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia , waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war .

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back.

Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.

"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."

Wu reported from Bangkok and Isachenkov from Moscow.

articles.title: Brasileiro morto em Israel é sepultado após 1 ano e 8 meses da morte | G1
articles.standfirst: Walid Khalid Abdalla Ahmad foi preso foi preso em 30 de setembro de 2024 em região ocupada por Israel e morreu em março de 2025. Brasileiro-palestino tinha 17 anos e não chegou a ser julgado.
articles.summary: Walid Khalid Abdalla Ahmad morreu aos 17 anos sob custódia israelense e o Itamaraty acusa Israel de violar o direito internacional ao reter o corpo por 20 meses.
articles.body:
O Ministério das Relações Exteriores informou nesta sexta-feira (13) que o brasileiro-palestino Walid Khalid Abdalla Ahmad, que morreu em custódia israelense em março de 2025 , foi sepultado nesta quinta-feira (12).

Como o sepultamento aconteceu 1 ano e 8 meses após a morte do brasileiro, o Itamaraty cobrou explicações por parte do governo de Israel , com o qual o governo brasileiro tem tido atritos públicos desde que o país passou a acusar a gestão de Benjamin Netanyahu de cometer genocídio na Faixa de Gaza.

"As condições às quais o cidadão brasileiro fora submetido durante seu encarceramento, assim como a retenção de seu corpo por quase 20 meses pelo governo israelense, constituíram flagrante violação do direito internacional humanitário", afirmou o Itamaraty.

"Durante todo o tempo de retenção do corpo, o Escritório de Representação do Brasil em Ramala e a Embaixada do Brasil em Tel Aviv realizaram repetidas gestões pela liberação e prestaram assistência à família", acrescentou.

Walid foi preso em 30 de setembro de 2024 na cidade de Silwad, na Cisjordânia, região ocupada por Israel . Acusado de agredir militares israelenses com pedras, ele não chegou a ser julgado antes de morrer.

De acordo com a Federação Árabe-Palestina do Brasil, a prisão em Megido, onde Walid estava preso, é conhecida pelo uso de tortura com choques elétricos, espancamentos e privação de comida.

A autópsia do jovem apontou como causa da morte “uma combinação de fome, desidratação por diarreia induzida por colite e complicações infecciosas, tudo agravado por desnutrição prolongada e privação de intervenção médica”.

Em março do ano passado, na nota em que confirma o falecimento de Walid Ahmad , o Itamaraty afirmou que as circunstâncias e a data exata do óbito ainda não haviam sido esclarecidas.

"O governo brasileiro tomou conhecimento, com profunda consternação, da morte do cidadão brasileiro Walid Khalid Abdalla Ahmad, de 17 anos, na prisão israelense de Megido. O menor, residente da Cisjordânia, no Estado da Palestina, fora detido em 30 de setembro de 2024 na Palestina ocupada e levado por forças israelenses à prisão de Megido, em território israelense", afirmou o Itamaraty na ocasião.

O cidadão brasileiro-palestino Walid Khalid Abdalla morreu em uma prisão em Megido, em Israel — Foto: Reprodução

Foi sepultado em 12 de novembro, em Silwad, na Cisjordânia, Estado da Palestina, o corpo do cidadão binacional brasileiro-palestino Walid Khalid Abdalla Ahmad, morto em custódia israelense em março de 2025, aos 17 anos de idade.

As condições às quais o cidadão brasileiro fora submetido durante seu encarceramento, assim como a retenção de seu corpo por quase 20 meses pelo governo israelense, constituíram flagrante violação do direito internacional humanitário.

O governo brasileiro ressalta a necessidade de explicação oficial conclusiva por parte do governo israelense sobre as causas do falecimento.

Durante todo o tempo de retenção do corpo, o Escritório de Representação do Brasil em Ramala e a Embaixada do Brasil em Tel Aviv realizaram repetidas gestões pela liberação e prestaram assistência à família.

O governo brasileiro renova condolências à família de Walid Khalid Abdalla Ahmad.

articles.title: Peltola extends lead after new Alaska Senate ballots count
articles.summary: In the last uncalled Senate race of 2026, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) gained an additional 5,000 newly counted votes Thursday and extended her lead o...
articles.body:
In the last uncalled Senate race of 2026, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) gained an additional 5,000 newly counted votes Thursday and extended her lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

Peltola leads Sullivan by 5,800 votes as of 9:30 a.m. EST Friday and surpassed Sullivan in the Alaska Beacon's calculation of how the vote will stand after the ranked choice votes are redistributed. If no candidate surpasses 50 percent of the vote, as is the current case, the race will be decided by ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18.

With more than 83 percent of the anticipated vote counted, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Peltola has maintained the lead she has had since Election Day even as the sprawling arctic state continues to count votes. She effectively declared victory following Thursday's ballot drop.

"As more ballots get counted, it is clear Mary's victory is all but guaranteed and Alaskans have resoundingly rejected Dan Sullivan's D.C. self dealing," the Peltola campaign posted to the social media platform X.

DDHQ has yet to call the race. Nevertheless, Peltola claimed she won Thursday's tabulated ballots by a 2-to-1 margin and that Sullivan is underperforming in traditionally conservative areas.

"When every vote is counted, Mary Peltola will be Alaska's next United States Senator," her campaign wrote in the post.

The Alaska Senate race turned into a national controversy after The New York Times revealed that Democrats were behind the campaign of Dan. J Sullivan Jr., a different candidate with the same name as the incumbent.

The Trump administration sued, attempting to block certification of the race if Peltola won by less than the amount of votes cast for the nonincumbent Sullivan. That lawsuit was eventually dismissed .

"Alaskans are ready for a Senator who fights to lower costs and take on DC corruption, and when every vote is counted, Mary will deliver for Alaska," Peltola's campaign posted to X.

Peltola surpassed the combined vote tally of both Sullivans earlier this week but has since dipped back below the combined vote count. President Trump has suggested all of Sullivan Jr.'s votes should be awarded to the incumbent Sullivan, claiming there is no other "fair solution."

articles.title: New congressman faces sexual harassment allegation
articles.summary: House Democrats are investigating an allegation of sexual harassment against Brian Poindexter, who defeated embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller.
articles.body:
Washington — House Democrats are investigating an allegation of sexual harassment against Brian Poindexter, who defeated embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller of Ohio in last week's elections.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, House Democrats' campaign arm, said Friday that it had hired an independent firm to investigate "any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts."

"The DCCC has been made aware of the allegations and takes them seriously," the group's executive director, Julie Merz, said in a statement.

A spokesperson for Poindexter's campaign characterized his actions as "an innocuous compliment to a volunteer."

"He heard later that it made her feel uncomfortable and he felt awful," the spokesperson said in a statement. "When Brian learned about this, we immediately began to work to get to the bottom of it with an outside HR firm. Neither Brian nor the campaign ever wants anyone to feel uncomfortable."

The investigation comes as Congress grapples with how to overhaul how it handles allegations of sexual misconduct as numerous lawmakers have faced complaints.

The DCCC was made aware of the allegations from two political action committees — the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC — which said they were informed of a report of alleged sexual harassment in the final days before the election.

"We informed the DCCC and connected the individual with legal advocacy and support services so she could determine how she wanted to proceed," the PACs said in a joint statement Friday. "The individual requested that we did not disclose any details about this publicly because she did not want her identity becoming public and she wanted an opportunity to determine how she wanted to proceed while protecting herself."

The PACs said they pulled their endorsements from Poindexter "pending the investigation being completed."

images.caption: New congressman faces sexual harassment allegation

articles.title: US gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requ...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requirement.

The requirement is scheduled to take effect nationally on Jan. 1, and states have been scrambling to put in place the staffing, training and technology to implement it by then. The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won't have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.

Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for lower-income people. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told state Medicaid directors on Friday that they'll still need to determine whether many enrollees and applicants for benefits are meeting new requirements that they are working, in school or volunteering.

The move announced Friday gives state social service departments more time to make sure complicated changes are ready to run before there are consequences. CMS said that states are making progress but have implementation challenges.

"I think these extra six months are going to give states the ability to respond to the change, and there will be fewer people that lose their coverage due to administrative failures" resulting from states' inability to prepare, Kathy Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told The Associated Press.

Still, she said it's not clear which states will opt to use the additional time.

Kate McEvoy, executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, said state Medicaid leaders "appreciate the additional flexibility that CMS is providing."

There's political pressure over the requirement

The decision also could give some breathing room to Congress to consider changes to the requirement. Democrats who are taking control of both chambers in January after their sweeping election victories last week have said they want to roll back the requirements.

The news comes after Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, of Oregon, and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, wrote to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz this week, asking to delay implementing the work reporting requirements. Their letter cites, in part, a recent decision out of a Boston federal court that determined medically frail people should not be bound by the work requirement qualification rules.

"The practical reality is that this significant implementation issue may not be definitively resolved for months, creating untenable uncertainty for states that need a final resolution of this issue before going live with work reporting requirements," the letter states. "The court ruling is an important victory for the millions of medically frail people who rely on Medicaid for their health care coverage."

Under the policy, many Medicaid beneficiaries must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month or be in school at least half-time. The new policy applies only to people who receive Medicaid under a voluntary expansion that 40 states undertook and which was intended to get health coverage to more lower-income adults who don't have kids at home. There are exceptions for those who are over 64, caring for kids under 14 or deemed too medically frail to work.

Critics say that most enrollees covered by the mandate are already working and that people are more likely to lose coverage because of the paperwork to prove it rather than failing to work.

The federal government is pushing states to use data from other government departments or elsewhere to verify whether beneficiaries are working as a way to reduce the burden on the beneficiaries to show proof.

Critics worry that the paperwork part will be the biggest issue

A few states have launched the work requirements early.

The first of them was Nebraska, where they started in May.

Preliminary data presented to the state's Medicaid Advisory Committee showed that more than 9 in 10 people subject to the work requirement and due to have their benefits renewed in July and August qualified.

But 533 people were denied continuing coverage. For most of them, it was over paperwork: They didn't show that they were working or were exempt from the requirement. Of those denied, 43 lost coverage because they did not meet the new requirement.

Similarly, most of the new Medicaid applicants who were denied coverage due to work requirements from May through August did not get the coverage because they did not provide information to verify whether they were complying.

Among both groups, it's not clear how many people didn't provide information because they weren't working — or how many might meet the requirements but failed to show it.

"There are likely people who are still eligible for coverage who lost it," said Amy Behnke, the CEO of the Health Care Center Association of Nebraska.

Trump International Airport in West Palm Beach, Fla., as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz listen.
