articles.title: FAA says nationwide ground stop is over after thousands of flights canceled
articles.summary: FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the United States.
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration announced that the nationwide ground stop it issued earlier on Friday has been lifted, nearly five hours after thousands of flights were canceled across the country.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a press conference Friday night that the airspace has reopened and some flights have started to take off, but warned that "it'll be slow."

"It's going to take us some time to unwind what happened this afternoon," he said.

Duffy said that "instability" in the radar communications at air traffic control centers began just after 3:30 p.m. ET. At the time, there were more than 3,500 planes in the air when the ground stop was issued —he blamed it on an "incredibly old air traffic system."

"We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said. "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded."

He went on to blame Congress for not providing the funds to update the outdated infrastructure.

"I can't build things if I don't have money," Duffy said.

Last year Congress approved $12.5 billion to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on, including old copper wires and radio systems. On social media, the GOP-controlled Senate Commerce Committee, which oversees the FAA, noted that "no new" air traffic area control centers have been built "since [Lyndon B. Johnson] was in office."

On Friday, Duffy asked for $50 billion from Congress to modernize the nation's air traffic control system. "This is bipartisan. This is American," he said.

He also didn't rule out the possibility of another outage due to the "analog" system. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can't wait for that," Duffy said.

When asked if he could say with certainty that the problem wasn't caused by a cyberattack, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said, "There is nothing certain right now. It doesn't appear that way."

Earlier in the day, Mullin told reporters that there was no reason to suspect a national security threat was behind the outage.

"There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for their loved ones," Mullin said.

"This is not another 9/11," he added. "This is a telecommunications outage; this is much different."

As news of the ground stop spread, Duffy wrote in a post on X , "The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

As of 9:30 p.m. ET, there were more than 25,100 flights delayed on Friday and more than 6,600 canceled within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware.com , a live flight tracker website.

There were more than 30,000 departures and arrivals scheduled for the remainder of the day, according to flight tracking app Flighty, the New York Times reported .

Airlines for America, an industry trade organization representing major U.S. airlines, wrote in a post on X , "Safety is always our top priority." It added that it's in communication with the Department of Transportation and the FAA. The association encouraged travelers to be in touch with their airline carrier for "real-time updates."

Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation into the nationwide ground stop.

"The safety of our skies is built on redundancies," she wrote on X in response to Duffy's update. "Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation. As Aviation Subcommittee Ranking Member, I'll be demanding answers from the FAA."

Citing multiple sources, CBS News reported Friday that "an update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage." It reported that the system is operated by L3Harris Technologies. The Wall Street Journal also reported that the outage appeared to be affecting the "telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies," which "handles crucial radio frequencies that air-traffic controllers use to communicate with pilots."

Microsoft said that its own global outage — from which it is still recovering — did not appear to be a factor. Mullin also said they weren't connected.

The National Weather Service told the New York Times that a viral screenshot claiming that its weather radar is down is "outdated," adding that it "has not experienced a disruption to its radar systems today."

Earlier this week, the FAA announced the nationwide rollout of a new $875 million artificial intelligence tool to help air-traffic controllers avoid delays. Called SMART — short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — it was made by an AI company called ASI and had previously been in use at Washington, D.C., airports since late September.

On social media, ASI said, "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."

A Yahoo reporter who was stuck on the tarmac on a United Airlines flight waiting to depart from Los Angeles International Airport passed along updates from the cabin. She said her pilot told passengers that "what happened was a communications outage that started in Kansas City Center, which is responsible for the airspace above the middle of America, and it spread nationwide."

She also said she received an update from United Airlines, which said, "Air traffic control is limiting the number of planes allowed to land and depart each hour in Los Angeles, affecting several flights. We're monitoring the situation closely to get you to your destination as soon as possible."

Around 7 p.m. ET, she said her flight "going over the Pacific" had departed. The New York Times has reported that "some international flights from the United States have been allowed to depart amid the ground stop." Alaska Airlines said in a statement that flights within Hawaii and Alaska have also been continuing, as have longer-distance flights to and from Honolulu.

Nationwide ground stops are pretty rare. The last time such an event occurred was in January 2023, when a pilot notification system went down. Before then, a nationwide ground stop was issued following the September 11, 2001, attacks.

articles.title: Rubio urges conservatives to uplift their ideology, brushes off Republicans’ midterm losses
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday downplayed Republicans’ devastating losses in the midterm elections, instead telling supporters, “Politics requires more than simply winning elections.”
articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday downplayed Republicans’ devastating losses in the midterm elections, instead telling supporters, “Politics requires more than simply winning elections.” “Those who believe that one setback, one defeat, one bad election spells the end of the republic should look to you as an example for inspiration,” Rubio said in his first major remarks since Election Day, given to the conservative Federalist Society at the National Lawyer’s Convention in Washington, D.C. Rubio, whose name has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, told the audience, “Great things that last are built in decades, not election cycles.” “There will be more victories, and there will be more defeats,” he said. “There will be more triumphs, and there will be more disappointments.” The secretary of state urged the crowd to remember that the government “is not the only source of political power” as he emphasized the importance of still uplifting conservative ideology despite election losses. Rubio pointed to power held by universities, the press and “the whole expanse of civil society.” “Elections decide who holds office for a season, but elections, they do not decide by themselves what our institutions teach or what our lawyers believe,” Rubio said. He also condemned the “endless barrage of claims about America’s alleged violations of international rules and norms,” including allegations that the U.S. had violated international law when striking boats allegedly used to traffic drugs in the Caribbean Sea or over the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies. Rubio also defended the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the continued war in Iran. “None of this has anything to do with any real higher standard of justice. It is a function of the people who control the official organs of global governance,” Rubio said. “For this global elite, international law is not a neutral body of rules. International law is an instrument, an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles.” Rubio denounced the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, saying, “Americans have never agreed to submit to the ICC’s authority, but that court and its allies in the global bureaucracy have appointed themselves judge and jury and executioner of the international order.” Last month, the Trump administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the ICC as part of its campaign to dismantle the court after it announced investigations into the U.S. Rubio on Friday also criticized “activist courts” on American soil, telling the crowd of lawyers, “The weaponization of international law is not altogether different from what we’ve seen here at home.” “The activist courts who seek to govern by injunction, twisting the law to fit whatever their preferences happen to be at any given place or time,” he said, adding that the judges are “allies” of those who have “denounced the Constitution.” “For these people, the fundamental purpose of the law, American law and international law alike, is to weaken the United States,” Rubio said. “It is to undermine our power as a sovereign nation to act. It is to hinder the American government’s ability to defend American interests at home and abroad.” Rubio’s words echo repeated attacks by President Donald Trump on judges who rule against his interests. The president has also increasingly clashed with the Supreme Court, which holds a 6-3 conservative majority and includes three justices appointed to the bench by Trump. The high court ruled against Trump this year on his tariff policies, his plan to diminish birthright citizenship, his efforts to interfere with mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections and his firing of a member of the Federal Reserve. After the Supreme Court’s ruling on his tariff policies, Trump called the justices a “disgrace to our nation.”

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China
articles.summary: White House says Trump plans to discuss the Iran war and nuclear arms at a meeting on the sidelines of APEC next week.
articles.body:
Leaders of the United States, China and Russia are set to hold an unprecedented three-way meeting next week, the White House has said.

US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China’s tech hub, the White House assistant press secretary confirmed in an announcement.

The talks will be held nine months after the last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow expired , leaving the world’s two countries with the largest atomic arsenals without caps for the first time in more than 50 years.

Trump has said the meeting is a chance for all three countries to reach a deal on nuclear stockpiles.

The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) lapsed in February. Trump then rejected Russia’s proposal to extend it for another year and demanded a “new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.

Expectations are low. “We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told the Reuters news agency, describing the meeting as the start of a conversation.

Russia holds the most nuclear warheads, followed by the US, then China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Trump plans on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to a senior US official who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity.

Elon Musk will also travel with Trump to China but will not attend the meeting, the official added. Trump is also not expected to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during the Asia trip.

The planned summit has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union shaped the post-war order.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, however, dismissed the parallel, saying any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be imposed on others, but he still called the meeting “extremely significant”.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced concern that the meeting could become a platform to discuss a Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back .

Trump has pursued closer ties with both leaders despite a short-lived trade war with China last year and Russia’s continuing war in Ukraine, where Washington is seeking to mediate a solution.

articles.title: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins the Alaska governor’s race
articles.summary: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won the Alaska governor’s race, NBC News projects, flipping control of the office from Republicans.
articles.body: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won the Alaska governor’s race, NBC News projects, flipping control of the office from Republicans. Kreiss-Tomkins’ victory marks the latest gain for Democrats at the state level in this year’s elections. The party will hold 30 governorships next year after flipping control in six states. At 37, Kreiss-Tomkins will be the youngest governor in Alaska history and next year he will be the youngest sitting governor in the country. Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, defeated three Republicans on the ballot to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy. In Alaska, the top four vote-getters in the primary regardless of party advance to the general election, where ranked choice voting is utilized. Kreiss-Tomkins secured a majority of the vote on the first ballot, so the ranked choice aspect did not come into play in the race. Former state Sen. Tom Begich, a Democrat, had finished second in the August primary just behind Kreiss-Tomkins. But he dropped out of the race soon after to consolidate Democratic support behind Kreiss-Tomkins. The three Republican candidates on the November ballot were Anchorage businesswoman Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former state Attorney General Treg Taylor. Wilson, who was backed by President Donald Trump, finished a distant second. Kreiss-Tomkins, who often goes by JKT in the state, earned bipartisan support during his campaign. Most notably, he was endorsed by GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski one week before Election Day. “JKT is a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now — a freshness of energy, a common-sense guy who has a known ability to be working together,” Murkowski said in an interview with NBC affiliate KTUU of Anchorage. Kreiss-Tomkins campaigned on boosting funding for public schools, lowering energy costs, expanding Medicaid and protecting Alaska’s fisheries. He also called for a moratorium on all new data centers until the state Legislature can pass regulations, and said he would not allow direct or indirect subsidies to data centers for electricity costs.

articles.title: Alaskans opt to stick with ranked choice voting
articles.summary: Alaskans have decided to stick with ranked choice voting, rejecting a ballot measure that sought to repeal the system, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Alaskans have decided to stick with ranked choice voting, rejecting a ballot measure that sought to repeal the system, NBC News projects. The unusual voting method was in the spotlight after a controversy around a potential spoiler candidate in the state’s competitive Senate race gathered steam in the final stretch of the election. In Alaska, candidates from all parties run on the same primary ballot, with the top four vote-getters advancing to the general election. Voters then rank those candidates in order of preference, and if no one eclipses the 50% threshold on the first ballot, the race goes to ranked choice tabulation. The fourth-place finisher is eliminated, and their supporters are redistributed based on how voters ranked the other candidates on the ballot. The process continues until a candidate reaches a majority. While supporters of the system say it gives more power to voters and incentivizes candidates to not only appeal to the most extreme elements of a party, critics argue it causes confusion. One week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan to run for Senate. Peltola and her campaign have denied pushing Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, to enter the race or being involved in his campaign. The episode is under federal and state investigation, though a federal judge earlier this month dismissed an effort by the Trump administration to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan. Ranked choice voting first went into effect in Alaska in 2022, after voters approved it through a ballot measure in 2020. A similar effort to repeal it failed by fewer than 800 votes in 2024. Open primaries and ranked-choice voting aren’t the only voting method that allow spoiler candidates. And supporters say that the method mitigates the effects by allowing voters to rank multiple candidates. Alaska and Maine are the only states that use ranked-choice voting for statewide elections.

articles.title: Democrat flips Alaska governor's mansion after Trump-backed GOP infighting
articles.summary: President Trump endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson for Alaska governor, but bitter GOP infighting and ranked-choice voting complicated the race to succeed Mike Dunleavy.
articles.body: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won Alaska's gubernatorial election, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson and flipping the governor's mansion. The Associated Press called the race for Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, Friday evening local time. He is the first Democratic governor in Alaska since 1998. Alaska's gubernatorial election became an unusual contest as Republicans battled among themselves over who should succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who was barred from seeking a third consecutive term. A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS Wilson, a conservative activist and former political operative, received President Donald Trump's endorsement during a campaign in which multiple Republicans competed for the governor's office. Trump publicly criticized fellow Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor, accusing them of dividing conservative voters and potentially jeopardizing the party's hold on the governorship. Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor, and Taylor, a former Alaska attorney general, remained part of the Republican field, creating a complicated general-election contest. ALASKAN POLITICAL SCION HOPES TO HOLD ONTO STATE'S SINGLE HOUSE SEAT Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, emerged as the Democratic contender, seeking to return his party to the governor's mansion after Dunleavy's two terms. The election unfolded under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. The process continues until a candidate secures a majority among continuing ballots. The system has added an unusual dynamic to Alaska politics, allowing multiple candidates from the same party to compete in the general election without a traditional partisan runoff.
